sections.h2: Selling a house in Peoria, AZ
sections.html:
Peoria lies northwest of Phoenix, and the city boundary crosses a county line. The county that holds your parcel determines who records your deed. The estimated population was 200,881 in July 2025, a 5.2 percent gain on the April 2020 estimate base.

The median owner-occupied home was valued at $463,600 for 2020 to 2024, and median gross rent was $1,843. Homeowners occupy 76.0 percent of homes. Peoria spans 176.08 square miles, so two Peoria houses can have different records, districts and rules. Your first job is to learn which ones apply to yours, and the sections below walk through each in turn, from county to permit to tax.

The bulk of the city is in Maricopa County. Its northern reach runs into Yavapai County, where a parcel answers to the Yavapai recorder, assessor and treasurer. Your tax statement shows which county bills you, and your title company can confirm it before you pick a closing date.

The same split touches schools. Peoria Unified School District covers the largest share. Deer Valley Unified serves parts of the northeast, Nadaburg Unified covers part of the northwest, and Wickenburg Unified serves the portion in Yavapai County. Get the school assignment for your address from the district itself. Memory is a poor source when a buyer is relying on it.

Peoria wants a city permit for any house run as a vacation or short-term rental. Ordinance 2022-20 sets the rule, following Arizona Senate Bill 1168, and the application is free. To keep a permit active, an owner must:

  • Notify surrounding neighbors and give them emergency contact information.
  • Carry liability insurance of at least $500,000 and run sex offender checks on guests, unless an online marketplace already provides them.
  • Show the city registration number in every advertisement.

Three verified violations inside a rolling 12 months, or a single serious infraction, can get a permit suspended for up to 12 months. To find out the permit status of a specific house, call the Code Compliance Division at 623-773-7162, and share what you learn with your buyer.

sections.h2: What to gather before accepting an offer
sections.html:
Having these in one folder can save days when an offer arrives:

  • The parcel number and the county it falls in, Maricopa or Yavapai
  • Any Peoria vacation rental permit number, with proof of the insurance behind it
  • Cooling system service records and the roof's repair history
  • Your newest property tax statement, so the title company can see what is paid
  • The school district name for the address, taken from the district itself

Summers here reach a record high of 122 degrees, which is why inspectors ask for cooling and roof records near the start.

For a parcel in Maricopa County, the Maricopa County Recorder takes the deed along with an Affidavit of Property Value or an exemption code, for the usual $30.00 per document. You can deliver it to 301 W Jefferson St, Suite 200 in Phoenix, mail it or send it electronically.

A.R.S. 11-1133 sets the affidavit rule. The form states the price, the parcel number, the sale date, how the buyer is financing and whether an owner or a tenant will live there. Without a complete form, and absent an exemption, the recorder has to turn the deed away. A Yavapai County parcel goes to that county's recorder, and your title company handles it.

sections.h2: If the house was a rental
sections.html:
A buyer looking at a permitted rental will have extra questions, and answers given early keep a deal calm. Keep the permit number, the insurance proof and a copy of your neighbor notice together. Say whether the permit was ever suspended, and what the city's rules ask of the next owner. A buyer who hears it from you trusts the rest of what you say.

Phone Code Compliance before you list. A permit in good standing is a plus for a buyer who plans to keep renting. If it is not in good standing, find out whether the problem can be cleared before escrow or whether the buyer must plan around it.

sections.h2: How the sale moves from offer to closing
sections.html:
Listing or cash, the sequence barely changes.

  1. Confirm your county, then confirm the school district for the address.
  2. Collect the permit, cooling, roof and tax papers from the list above.
  3. Accept an offer and open escrow.
  4. Escrow staff request payoff numbers on your loans and liens, work out each side's share of the year's tax and draft the deed with its affidavit.
  5. On closing day the deed goes to the recorder for the right county.
  6. Once it is recorded and payoffs are settled, you receive your proceeds.

A cash buyer needs no loan approval or lender appraisal, so those weeks of waiting disappear. The county question, the rental permit and the tax split stay, since they come with the house whoever pays for it.

Owe tax on the house? Say so up front. Past-due tax can be paid out of your proceeds, provided escrow has the figure before the closing date. Ask the treasurer for a current payoff rather than estimating.

sections.h2: Who to call and what to ask
sections.html:
Four calls cover nearly everything a Peoria seller needs to know.

  • Your title company: which county records the deed, and what it needs for the affidavit.
  • The Code Compliance Division, 623-773-7162: whether a rental permit is active.
  • The school district for your address: the assigned school, in the district's own words.
  • The county treasurer: whether the first half of the tax is paid and what is owed.

Write down the date and the answer from each call. If a buyer later asks why you said something about the permit or the school, your notes settle it quickly. Do this in the first week, before you take showings or an offer, since each office can take a day or two to answer.

Peoria's size is the reason for the care. The city covers more than 176 square miles and had 190,985 people at the 2020 count, so a neighbor's house may sit under a different district or even a different county than yours.

Tax bills here split into two halves, per A.R.S. 42-18052.

Payment optionDue dateDelinquent after
First halfOctober 15:00 p.m. on November 1
Second halfMarch 15:00 p.m. on May 1

The treasurer in your parcel's county can tell you whether the first half is paid. Your title company then works out the buyer's and seller's shares for the year. A bill of $100 or less is due in full on October 1.

faqs.q: Does Peoria require a permit to rent a house short term?
faqs.a: Yes. Peoria's Ordinance 2022-20 requires a city permit for vacation and short-term rentals. The application is free, and owners must meet notification, insurance and advertising rules.

faqs.q: Is all of Peoria in Maricopa County?
faqs.a: No. Most of it is, but the northern part of the city extends into Yavapai County. That decides which county recorder, assessor and treasurer handle your parcel.

faqs.q: What is the median home value in Peoria?
faqs.a: For 2020 to 2024 the Census Bureau reports $463,600 for owner-occupied homes citywide. Any single house can sit well above or below that figure.
Peoria Unified School District serves most of the city. Deer Valley Unified, Nadaburg Unified and Wickenburg Unified cover other portions, so check your address with the district.

faqs.q: Does a Peoria deed need an Affidavit of Property Value?
faqs.a: Yes, unless the transfer qualifies for an exemption code. The recorder will not record a deed without the affidavit unless an exemption is noted.
